introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; filigranes gcerevision ignorés. Le texte de la page 2 transparaît en miroir sur la page de garde (verso mal opacifié) et quelques espaces sont manquants à l'impression (question 8 : « between1871and1890 », rétabli en « between 1871 and 1890 ») ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation n'est inventée et les chiffres sont limités à des repères datés de l'historiographie courante (dates, traités) ; à relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 4 : l'énoncé imprimé date le déclenchement de la révolte Mau Mau de 1951. L'historiographie situe la montée de la violence en 1950-52 (mouvement interdit en août 1950, état d'urgence proclamé le 20 octobre 1952) ; le sujet est recopié tel quel et le corrigé précise la chronologie sans corriger l'énoncé.

Question 5 : l'Afrique équatoriale française regroupe le Gabon, le Moyen-Congo, l'Oubangui-Chari et le Tchad ; le Cameroun, ancien mandat puis tutelle, n'en faisait pas partie. Les interventions militaires françaises (Gabon 1964, Tchad à partir de la fin des années 1960, Centrafrique 1979) et le rôle du réseau Foccart sont cités selon l'historiographie courante, sans chiffres.

Question 7 : le sujet emploie « romanisation » au sens de la promotion du catholicisme romain par Jacques II ; les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, acquittement des sept évêques et invitation à Guillaume le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre).

Question 9 : le montant des réparations (132 milliards de marks-or, fixé en 1921) et les pertes territoriales sont cités de mémoire historique établie ; aucune statistique de population n'est avancée.

Question 11 : la Banque mondiale et le FMI sont des institutions spécialisées de l'ONU ; l'UNICEF (fonds et non institution spécialisée) n'est volontairement pas traité. Les dates (variole déclarée éradiquée en 1980, Alma-Ata 1978, convention 182 de l'OIT en 1999, Codex Alimentarius 1963, retrait des États-Unis de l'UNESCO en 1984-85) sont citées selon l'historiographie courante.

Question 12 : le sujet vise la rupture sino-soviétique après la mort de Staline (1953). Les dates (discours de Khrouchtchev en février 1956, rupture de l'accord nucléaire en 1959, retrait des conseillers en 1960, congrès de Bucarest en juin 1960, guerre sino-indienne 1962, incidents de l'Oussouri en mars 1969) sont données selon l'historiographie courante ; aucun chiffre n'est avancé.

Thèmes : les noms sont qualifiés pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone (`sino-soviet split`, `afrikaner nationalism`, `mau mau revolt in kenya`...) ; plusieurs sont réutilisés des sujets History 2020-2021 (`scramble for africa`, `apartheid in south africa`, `cold war`, `indirect rule in colonial africa`) ; à revérifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
"Apartheid was adopted in South Africa in 1948 largely because of the economic interests of the Boers." Discuss.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Apartheid ("apartness") was the policy of racial separation and white domination put into law by the National Party (NP) after it won the general election of May 1948 under D. F. Malan. The "Boers" in the question are the Afrikaners, the Afrikaans-speaking descendants of the Dutch settlers. The statement claims that apartheid was mainly the product of their economic interests. Economic motives were important, but they cannot fully explain apartheid, which also came from Afrikaner nationalism, religion, history, fear of African political and social power, and the existing tradition of racial segregation. The statement is therefore only partly true.

**1. Economic interests of the Afrikaners (the case for the statement).**
- *Poor whites and the Afrikaner economic position.* Many Afrikaners had been poor, mostly rural people since the Boer War (1899-1902) and the depression of the 1930s; many had moved to the towns, where they competed with cheap African labour. Job reservation and the colour bar were meant to protect white workers and give Afrikaners advancement.
- *Farmers' need for cheap African labour.* During and after the Second World War industry expanded and many Africans moved to the towns, causing a labour shortage on white farms, which were a main support of the NP. Apartheid, with its pass laws and influx control, aimed to control African movement and keep labour available for farms and mines.
- *Afrikaner capital.* Afrikaner business organisations (such as banking and insurance companies and the economic movement of the 1930s and 1940s) grew and expected state help; control of the state allowed them to share in the economy previously dominated by English-speaking capital.
- *Economic competition.* African urbanisation, strikes (such as the African mineworkers' strike of 1946) and growing African trade unions seemed a threat to white jobs and wages.

**2. Other factors (the limits of the statement).**
- *Afrikaner nationalism and history.* Memories of British rule, the Boer War and the concentration camps, the Great Trek and the centenary celebrations of 1938, and the fight to protect the Afrikaans language and identity created a strong nationalism, expressed through organisations such as the Broederbond and parties such as the NP.
- *Ideology and religion.* Many Dutch Reformed Church leaders and Afrikaner intellectuals taught that God had created separate peoples and that the races should be kept apart; this gave apartheid a moral and religious justification.
- *Fear of racial mixing and of African power.* The "swart gevaar" (black peril) and fear of being swamped by an African majority led whites to want absolute control. Laws such as the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act (1949), the Immorality Amendment Act (1950) and the Population Registration Act (1950) have nothing to do with economic gain alone.
- *Political context and continuity.* The Fagan Commission (appointed in 1946, report in 1948) accepted that African urbanisation could not be reversed, while the Sauer Report (1947) of the NP recommended strict separation, and the NP presented apartheid as the alternative to the United Party's weak segregation policy. The NP, with its ally the Afrikaner Party, won a majority of seats in 1948 even though it had fewer votes than its rivals, and the white electorate also feared communism and the rising African, Indian and Coloured resistance (the ANC Youth League, 1944). Segregation had existed earlier (the Natives Land Act of 1913, Urban Areas Act of 1923), so apartheid was an intensification of a tradition and not only a response to a new economic situation.
- *Economic interests were not only Afrikaner interests.* English-speaking mine owners and industrialists also benefited from cheap African labour, which shows that economic motives were not confined to the Boers.

**3. Evaluation.** Economic interests (control of labour, protection of white jobs, advancement of Afrikaner capital) were a significant reason why apartheid was adopted and why it took the form of pass laws, job reservation and the Group Areas Act (1950). But "largely" is too strong: race ideology, nationalism, religion and fear of African political challenge were at least equally important, and they explain features, such as the ban on mixed marriages, that had no economic purpose.

**Conclusion.** Apartheid was adopted in 1948 through a combination of economic, political, ideological and historical causes. The economic interests of the Afrikaners were one of the main causes, but not the only one, so the statement overstates their role.
